title: Revealed: profiles of UK experts on gambling harm being hijacked to push illegal online casinos
text:
Prof Heather Wardle has dedicated 20 years to researching the harm caused by gambling.
So the University of Glasgow social scientist was horrified to learn that her reputation and even her photograph had been hijacked by rogue casinos claiming her endorsement for the very games whose addictive properties she has documented.
“I would never review these things and promote them to people,” she said. “It’s completely out of kilter with the research I’ve conducted across my entire career.”
Wardle is far from alone in being targeted like this, evidence reviewed by the Guardian suggests.
At least six prominent academics appear to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Most appear to be “affiliates”, businesses that earn commission by directing online traffic towards gambling firms. Several of the websites promoted unlicensed casinos that are not on GamStop, a UK scheme to help people suffering from problem gambling shut themselves out of betting sites.
Nor is it just academics whose public profile appears to have been misused in this way. Dozens of websites with no previous links to betting appear to have been bought up on the cheap and redesigned, capitalising on their existing search engine recognition.
The result is that people visiting what they think is a site dedicated to politics, tourism or even HIV research, can end up being lured in by offshore casinos.
The findings highlight not just the unscrupulous tactics used by the multibillion-pound illicit market but also the enormous challenge facing the UK authorities.
‘It’s completely egregious’
One site, called 666 Casino, features a photo of a smiling Wardle, described as “the woman behind the reviews”.
“Every trustworthy casino review needs someone who’s actually done the legwork, and that’s precisely the role Heather Wardle has carved out for herself in the UK gambling content space,” it reads.
In a lengthy “biography”, the page claims she began as a casual online gambler but later began analysing and rating the best casinos, including the quality of their bonuses and the speed of cash withdrawals.
“I was saddened but I wasn’t surprised,” said Wardle. “Some quarters of the gambling industry will go far to undermine academics who are doing work in the public interest.”
Wardle is one of at least six prominent academics whose reputations, built on their research into how gambling can exploit and harm people, have been co-opted in this way. All told the Guardian they had not consented and were alarmed by the use of their names and images.
“It’s a deliberate misuse of our profiles to mislead consumers into believing that these products, which are objectively the most harmful, are safe,” said Wardle.
The social scientist has been forced to write to the organisations that help fund her work, many of whom do on strict conditions governing any engagement she might have with the gambling sector, assuring them that her name is being used without consent.
Academics at the universities of Swansea, Loughborough and Bristol have also been targeted. Some of the wording on the sites appeared to have been generated using AI, the academics said.
“It takes years to build up an academic reputation, and only a few lines of this AI slop to damage it,” said Prof Gerda Reith, another victim of identity misuses, who also works at the University of Glasgow.
The aim of hijacking these academics’ profile, it appears, is to convince people to part with their money by clicking on links to casinos.
Of the casinos the Guardian viewed, none had a licence to operate in the UK and appear, therefore, to be doing so illegally.
“It’s completely egregious,” said Wardle.
Hall of mirrors
In practice, a lack of transparency about who owns and operates websites means that tracking down who is behind this phenomenon can be dizzying.
Of 28 websites purloining the names of British academics, including 666 Casino, most appeared to be registered in Ukraine.
A contact page for 666 Casino claims it is owned by a Malta-based business with a licence from the UK Gambling Commission. This appears to be untrue.
The site gives a London address but appears to have no connection to any companies registered there. A link to Google Maps shows an address in Sydney, Australia.
Casino games advertised on the site, such as Wild Lady Cash and Lucky 100 Bells, redirect players to a website called Elite Spin, whose Trustpilot page states that the site is based in Canada. Elsewhere on the internet, casino review pages claim Elite Spin is licensed in Costa Rica.
When the Guardian tried to contact 666 Casino via an email address provided on its website, the email bounced back.
This international hall of mirrors is typical of illicit casino operations, including some previously exposed by the Guardian.
It is not just academic reputations that appear to have been co-opted.
Jonathan Harbourne, the founder of the LGBT History Project, a volunteer-run national heritage archive, became suspicious after one of the community-led archive’s former web addresses was taken over.
He has since identified about 40 websites that appear, like the academics, to have been misused for the benefit of rogue casinos.
They include a hospital trust, an Italian restaurant in Croydon and the home of the Labour party in the now defunct London constituency of Hornsey and Wood Green.
They also include Sigma Research, part of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine dedicated to researching HIV and sexual health.
Harbourne said: “Once an address has belonged to a hospital, a charity or a council, it should not be possible to buy it and fill it with casino adverts aimed at people who have asked to be excluded from gambling.”
Most of the sites were auctioned by a small company called DomainLore, which trades in expired UK domains.
A spokesperson for DomainLore said it – and other auction companies – could neither make “speculative judgments” about how the domains they sell might be used, nor police their use after a sale.
“Responsibility for how a domain is used rests with the registrant,
 
not with the marketplace that facilitated the registration or sale,” they said.
The company that deals with those registrants is Nominet, which handles the registration of UK domain names.
Harbourne thinks Nominet, armed with the knowledge of who is registering the pages, could and should be doing more to address the problem.
Nominet said it was working with the authorities including the Gambling Commission, which could request data about who was behind such sites.
“Since July, 140 domains have been suspended following requests from the Gambling Commission,” said a Nominet spokesperson.
New powers
As fast as the sites come down, they come back up, reflecting the wider issue of a fast-growing illicit market targeting UK consumers.
The Betting and Gaming Council (BGC), which lobbies on behalf of licensed operators, estimates that £33bn will be wagered on unlicensed sites by 2028.
The BGC, of course, has an incentive to play up the risks of illicit operators, an important plank of its argument against tougher regulation and higher taxes.
But the growing risk to UK consumers is being taken seriously by the government. It has given the Gambling Commission £26m over three years to fund measures including an illegal betting taskforce.
A spokesperson for theregulator said it was now conducting “one of the largest anti-illegal market operations anywhere in the world”.
In the first six months of this year, it has issued more than 1,000 cease and desist letters to advertisers and gambling operators, disrupted or geo-blocked 1,688 websites and referred more than 2,000 to search engines to be delisted.
By the end of the year, the Gambling Commission is also expected to get new powers to take down websites through the courts under the Crime and Policing Act 2026.
It is unclear how effective these powers will be. In the meantime, there appears to be very little that can be done to stop rogue casinos stealing the identities of those who have made a career of tackling gambling harm.
